draft.title: Planning for life stages
card: Money needs change as a person's life changes. A plan that suits one stage may not suit the next.
At school, income is often small, such as pocket money or a part-time job. Spending is usually on phones, food and fun, and saving may be for a first car or a trip.
Starting work and renting adds regular income, but also rent, bills, transport and tax. Raising a family adds new costs, such as food, child care and a larger home.
Near retirement, the aim moves to having enough money to live on once work income stops. Example: Sam earns $900 a week and pays $350 rent. A new baby adds costs, so Sam must change the plan.
draft.remember: Life changes, so money needs change, and a good plan is updated to match.

a.q: Why should a person review their money plan when they move from school to full-time work and renting?
opts: Their income and expenses have changed
Their old plan will no longer be legal
They no longer need to save any money
Their expenses will stay the same as before
a.why: Full-time work brings regular income, and renting adds costs such as rent and bills. The old plan was built for a different situation. Expenses do not stay the same, so that option is wrong.
a.clue: Think about what is new in income and costs.

b.q: Priya has just had her first child. Her family now pays for child care and nappies. What should she do with her money plan?
opts: Update it to include the new costs
Keep it exactly the same as before
Ignore it until she retires
Remove all savings goals from now on
b.why: A new child adds regular costs, so the plan needs to change to cover them. Keeping it the same could leave her short. Savings goals may be adjusted, but they do not have to be removed.
b.clue: Her costs have changed, so her plan should too.

a.best: Their income and expenses have changed

b.best: Update it to include the new costs

problems.detail: The Sam example (new baby, rent) sits in the retirement bullet, but it shows the family stage. Students may link the example to retirement planning. It belongs with the family bullet.
'Starting work and renting adds regular income' suggests renting brings income. Only starting work adds income; renting adds costs.
The clue 'Think about what is new in income and costs' repeats the wording of the right option, so it points straight to the answer.
The clue 'Her costs have changed, so her plan should too' states the answer outright.
The distractors ('will no longer be legal', 'no longer need to save any money') are implausible. Year 11 students can pick the answer without understanding the idea.
The distractors ('Ignore it until she retires', 'Keep it exactly the same') are obviously wrong. The question tests little beyond common sense.

check.summary: The facts are sound, but the Sam family example is misplaced in the retirement bullet, and the card wrongly implies renting adds income. Both clues give the answers away, and the implausible distractors make the questions too easy.

proposal.title: Planning for life stages
card: Money needs change as life moves from school to work, renting, family and retirement. A plan that suits one stage may not suit the next.
At school, income is often small, such as pocket money or a part-time job. Starting full-time work brings a regular wage. Moving out to rent adds costs such as rent, bills and transport.

A family adds costs such as child care, nappies and a larger home. Income may fall if a parent works less. Example: Sam earns $900 a week and pays $350 rent, and a new baby means Sam's plan needs to change.
Near retirement, the aim moves to having enough to live on once work income stops, such as from superannuation and savings.
proposal.remember: Each life stage can change both income and costs, so review the plan at each change.

a.q: Leo finishes school, starts a full-time job and moves into a rented flat. How do his money needs change?
opts: Income rises, and costs such as rent and bills begin
Income rises, so he no longer needs to plan spending
Costs rise, but his income stays at part-time levels
Income stays the same, but rent replaces fun spending
a.why: A full-time job brings a regular wage, usually more than school income, and renting adds rent, bills and transport. A higher income does not remove the need for a plan, because the new costs still have to fit within it.
a.clue: Look at what comes in and what goes out.

b.q: Priya and her partner have their first child. Priya will work part-time for a year. Which change to their plan fits this stage?
opts: Plan for new costs and a lower income for a while
Plan for new costs while income stays the same
Plan for lower costs, as she will be home more
Plan to live on super, as her work income stops
b.why: A baby adds costs such as child care and nappies, and part-time work means Priya earns less, so the plan must cover both. Planning only for the new costs is the tempting mistake, because it misses the drop in income.
b.clue: Part-time work changes more than her hours.

a.best: Income rises, and costs such as rent and bills begin

b.best: Plan for new costs and a lower income for a while
